match.reason: The brief covers fascist rule in both Italy and Germany, including propaganda and rebuilding the army, but both bank points cover only Mussolini's rise in Italy, so they are narrower than the new point.

draft.title: The rise of fascism
card: Fascism was a movement led by a strong dictator who demanded total loyalty to the nation. Mussolini in Italy and Hitler in Germany were fascist leaders.
They won support by playing on fear, such as fear of poverty, disorder and enemies at home and abroad. They also promised to make the nation proud and strong again.
They used propaganda, which is information shaped to win people's support. Posters, rallies, newspapers and radio spread their message.
Once in power, they crushed opposition by banning rival parties and silencing critics. They also built up their armies.
draft.remember: Fascist leaders won power with fear, nationalism and propaganda, then crushed opposition.

opts: Information shaped to win support for a cause
A law that bans all rival political parties
A secret police force that arrests critics
A plan to build up the army in peacetime
a.why: Propaganda spreads a message through posters, rallies and radio to win support. Banning rival parties is something leaders did after gaining power, which is a different step.
a.clue: Think of posters and radio broadcasts.

b.q: A leader promises to make his nation proud again and blames outsiders for its problems. Which tool of fascist leaders is this?
opts: Nationalism combined with fear
Crushing opposition with bans
Building up the army
Giving up power peacefully
b.why: Pride in the nation is nationalism, and blaming outsiders plays on fear. Banning critics and building armies came after a leader held power, and nothing here describes them.
b.clue: The leader is still trying to win people over.

a.best: Information shaped to win support for a cause

problems.detail: The right option uses the word 'nationalism', but the card never uses or explains it. The card only says leaders 'promised to make the nation proud and strong again'. The term appears only in the remember line, so some students may not link it to the card.
The distractor 'Giving up power peacefully' is plainly not something fascist leaders did. That leaves fewer believable choices, so students can rule it out without knowing the idea.
